👤3 · The avatar — F.R.E.D.

Every one of the five talks to the same man. He is never named or described directly — he's constructed entirely out of symptoms and failed attempts.

Who he is, in their words

A man past fifty, up three to seven times a night. Standing at the toilet waiting for a stream to start. Still dripping after he zips up. Never feels empty. He has already tried saw palmetto, cutting coffee, drinking less, eating better, exercising — and been to a doctor who handed him Flomax.

Underneath the bathroom problem is the real one, which the scripts name only glancingly and never dwell on: the bedroom. “Morning salute.” “Kill your sex drive.” “Bedroom performance issues.” The urinary symptom is the permissible complaint. The sexual one is the engine.

He is addressed as “guys” — never as a patient, never by a demographic label.

Fears

Catheters. Surgery. Losing erections permanently. Wetting himself in public. Becoming an old man in front of his wife.

Results wanted

Sleep through the night. A stream “like you're in your 30s.” Empty the bladder in one go. Stop planning his day around toilets.

Expectations

Low. He has been sold to before and it didn't work. He expects another pill, another temporary fix, another lighter wallet.

Desires

To feel capable again. To not be managed, medicated, or operated on. To fix it himself, privately, without another appointment.

🪜4 · The pain ladder

Every script climbs the same staircase — nuisance first, catastrophe last. The bar length is the severity of the consequence, not a measured value.

Man boobs · belly fat · mood swings · memory loss · low libido1128533
Wetting yourself · can't make it to the bathroom in time2612234
Infection · “peeing out painful burning lava”2628920
Catheter “shoved up your penis” · 2 litres of urine trapped2628920 · C ads
Surgery · scalpel scraping the prostate · 40% lose their morning salute4 of 5
“Your bladder can burst. And yes, that can kill you.”C ads

The “40%” figure and the “research from Harvard” attribution appear in four ads with no citation anywhere. Treat both as unsourced.

🧱5 · The shared skeleton

All three bodies run the same six beats in the same order. If you write new creative, this is the structure to fill — not a blank page.

BEAT 1

Curiosity hook

An everyday thing (eggs, sex, coffee) attached to his condition. Zero selling. Buys 3 seconds.

BEAT 2

Negation stack

Rapid-fire dismissal of everything he's tried. “Saw palmetto? Nope. Flomax? No.” Signals I know your history.

BEAT 3

The real cause reveal

“Prostate problems have nothing to do with the prostate.” Reframes him as misinformed, not failed.

BEAT 4

Named mechanism + prop

A coined term and a physical model on camera. The prop is doing as much work as the words.

BEAT 5

Agitate to catastrophe

Play the consequence forward: catheter, surgery, impotence, death. This is the longest beat in every script.

BEAT 6

Frictionless exit

“Free. No email required. 30 seconds. At home. No doctor.” Every objection pre-answered. Double CTA.

🚦7 · Compliance heat

Scored against Meta's published Advertising Standards. Every ad in the set has at least one named-violation pattern.

AdRiskWhy
1128533▲ High Hook asserts the viewer's condition · “shrink your prostate” · “practically overnight” · off-platform push framed as evading social media
2628920▲ High Condition asserted at viewer · graphic surgical and catheter imagery · same off-platform framing
2612234▲ High “the hidden reason you keep getting up at night” · names prescription drugs · unsourced 40% stat · 30-second cure
2629927▲▲ Very high “that can kill you” · catheter imagery · condition asserted · unsourced Harvard claim · 30-second cure
2636498▲▲ Very high Identical script to 2629927
What only the frames show
  • 2629927 carries an on-screen disclaimer: “Dramatization using an AI-generated performer.” The presenter may be synthetic. Worth confirming before any creative leans on this doctor's authority.
  • There are two different presenters, not one. Body A is a male doctor speaking as himself. Body C's narrator is a woman in a white coat citing him third-hand. Same funnel, two faces.
  • 2629927 opens on a big-prostate/small-prostate diagram. That's before/after visual grammar, which Meta's health policy names directly. It also sits under the words “shrink a swollen prostate.”
♻️8 · What to take, what to leave
Steal this
  • The negation stack. Naming what he's already tried, and dismissing it in four seconds, is the strongest trust move in the set.
  • A coined mechanism name. “The prostate plug” gives him a thing to point at. Every winning body has one.
  • The physical prop. A model on camera carries the explanation and creates the visual suspense your own framework asks for.
  • The friction stack at the CTA. Free · no email · 30 seconds · at home · no appointment. Every objection answered before it forms.
  • Hook rotation. Keep the winning body fixed, vary the opener. They're already doing this — match it.
Leave this
  • Hooks that assert his condition. “your swollen prostate” is structurally Meta's own banned example. Say “a swollen prostate.”
  • “Shrink,” “kills the bacteria,” “eradicate.” Disease-treatment claims on a supplement — Meta and the FTC both.
  • “That can kill you.” Sensational content, and the ceiling on agitation isn't worth the account.
  • The censorship framing. Telling viewers the real content is banned from social is the single most dangerous line in the set.
  • Unsourced stats. The 40% figure and “Harvard” need a citation or they need to go.
Section 2

Hook request — 75 pre-intro hooks

Now that we know exactly what we're working with, here's what's next.
25 per base ad, across five templates. Each is a 2–5 second scene bolted onto the front of an existing ad.

🧾Receipts — these are already running
Receipts

This isn't a theory. It's already printing money.

Every ad below was written by Michael at Sculpt Nation — and they're all still running today.

Why "still running" is the whole argument. In direct response, longevity is the proof. A losing ad gets killed in days. An ad still live months later is an ad that's still profitable — the algorithm has voted, over and over, with real money. These aren't case studies. They're survivors.
The Task 1 template — and the blood sugar angle, already proven
"I didn't know what CHICKEN does to BLOOD SUGAR LEVELS"
This is the exact format Task 1 is built on — and look at the marker: blood sugar. Michael already ran this angle at Sculpt Nation and it's still running. We're not inventing a technique or gambling on a new angle. We're re-deploying a proven, still-live winner into a new vertical.

The construction: "I didn't know what [everyday food] does to [scary marker]." Both slots are things the viewer trusts. It never reveals the direction of the answer — it just opens the loop and lets the gap do the work.

Food-as-villain
Greek Yogurt & Berries
Take an everyday food the viewer trusts — the healthiest thing in their fridge — and attach a threat to it. Same machine we're now pointing at blood sugar: the oatmeal, the fruit, the yogurt.
View in Meta Ad Library ↗
Same template, different marker
"…what EGGS do to CORTISOL"
Proof the format isn't a one-off — swap the food, swap the marker, and it keeps working. Eggs → cortisol. Chicken → blood sugar. The template is the asset.
View in Meta Ad Library ↗
The visual half of the formula
Same ad, new imagery
Look at the shot: the eggs are being blowtorched. The food isn't just named — something weird is done to it on camera. Everyday food + wrong action + "wait, what?"

Don't shoot a stock bowl of oatmeal. Torch it. Squish it. Pour sugar over it.
View in Meta Ad Library ↗
▸ Different vertical (supplements vs men's prostate health), so the claims don't transfer — but the mechanics do: fear in the first second, an everyday object as the villain, debunk-the-myth, and a visual that makes you go "wait, what?"
⚙️The mechanic

A pre-intro hook is a 2–5 second scene bolted onto the front of an existing ad. It stops the scroll, opens a curiosity loop, ends by pointing at the ad, and hands into the ad's real first line. The hook only opens the loop — it never answers it. The ad does that.

Every line is first-person — “I didn't know…”, “I thought…”, “I spent…”. Never a promise to the viewer, never a claim about them. That's what keeps it runnable.

Shoot the object, not the talking head. Pair the line with something being done to the thing on camera — torched, squeezed, poured on. The line opens the loop; the visual earns the “wait, what?”

✍️ Written by Michael

🎥Before you shoot
Writers
  • Keep it first-person. “I didn't know”, “I thought”, “I spent”. The moment it becomes “you”, it's a claim about the viewer.
  • Never answer the loop. The hook's only job is to make them need the next three seconds.
  • Talk about prostates, not your prostate. Plural and general. Shorter, and it stays out of trouble.
Editors
  • Something happens to the object. Torch the eggs, crimp the hose, plug the sink. A line over a face is half a hook.
  • Cut hard into the base ad. No fade, no beat. The last word of the hook runs straight into the ad's first line.
  • Best seams: coffee lines → Base C · garden hose → Base B · eggs → Base A. Those splice invisibly.
